title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Armored Likho digging a snake pit: inside the covert BusySnake Stealer campaign

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-03 17 use cases 11 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An inside look at the active Armored Likho APT campaign. The attackers are using spear-phishing, AI-generated loaders, and a new Python-based tool, BusySnake Stealer, to target organizations in Russia, Kazakhstan, and Brazil.

CVEsCVE-2025-9491
ATT&CKT1027 T1047 T1053.005 T1059.001 T1176 T1190 T1204.002 T1218.011 T1555.003 T1566 T1566.001

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ZDI-CAN-25373 (CVE-2025-9491) LNK spawning PowerShell to fetch BusySnake loader · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Armored Likho digging a snake pit: inside the covert BusySnake Stealer campaign
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BusySnake NSIS dropper: pnx.exe injected from Temp\ns*.tmp staging folder · [LLM] BusySnake Python stealer executed from %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper (module.pyw) · [LLM] BusySnake VBScript persistence: wh_selfdelete.vbs / run.vbs in WindowsHelper · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BusySnake reverse SSH tunnel: ssh.exe -R launched by bundled Python payload · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
BusySnake NSIS dropper: pnx.exe injected from Temp\ns*.tmp staging folder AIInstallation High
Hunts the Armored Likho NSIS self-extracting dropper (e.g. psihologicheskiy_test.exe) writing and launching the legitimate binary pnx.exe from its temporary ns*.tmp extraction directory, into which the malicious loader is code-injected. This is article-specific because pnx.exe running out of an NSIS Temp folder is the first on-host execution artifact of this chain. Rationale: Anchors on the exact article string $temp\nsn5531.tmp\pnx.exe generalised to the NSIS ns*.tmp pattern; pnx.exe executing from an NSIS temp folder is a narrow, high-fidelity artifact of this dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/armored-likho-targets-government.html • https://www.securityweek.com/armored-likho-apt-targeting-government-electric-power-entities/
ATT&CKT1055 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Panasonic/other software shipping a 'pnx.exe' from a permanent install path (excluded here by the Temp\ns*.tmp path anchor)
  • Security researcher/malware analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox VM
  • NSIS-based legitimate installers that coincidentally extract a binary named pnx.exe to Temp
  • EDR test/red-team emulation of this exact chain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the pnx.exe hash against the sample and identify the parent NSIS SFX (e.g. psihologicheskiy_test.exe) and the originating archive/email. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the pnx.exe process tree, and preserve the ns*.tmp folder for forensics before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper creation, module.pyw, run.vbs/wh_selfdelete.vbs, and outbound GitHub payload pulls; sweep the fleet for the same pnx.exe path.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pnx.exe"
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\Temp\\ns[a-z0-9]+\.tmp\\pnx\.exe$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\Temp\\ns[a-z0-9]+\.tmp\\pnx\.exe$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BusySnake Python stealer executed from %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper (module.pyw) AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the BusySnake Stealer primary payload — module.pyw run by a bundled Python 3.12 interpreter from the malware's %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper working directory. This is article-specific: the actor stages its own python.exe/pythonw.exe, get-pip.py and module.pyw under WindowsHelper and runs the .pyw headless. Rationale: Anchors on the exact staging path $appdata\WindowsHelper and the payload filename module.pyw; a self-contained Python interpreter running a .pyw from an AppData WindowsHelper folder is not seen in benign software. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/armored-likho-targets-government.html • https://gbhackers.com/busysnake-stealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool coincidentally installed to a folder literally named WindowsHelper (rare)
  • Developer running an embedded/portable Python distribution from an AppData path for a personal script
  • Malware analyst re-running the extracted payload in a lab
  • Software using PyInstaller/embedded Python that names a script module.pyw (very rare)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","pycharm64.exe","devenv.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture module.pyw and the WindowsHelper directory contents, confirm PyArmor packing and the bundled python.zip/get-pip.py provenance. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the pythonw.exe tree, and disable/delete the associated 5-minute scheduled task. 3) Hunt: pull browser-credential and cookie access on the host (Firefox/Chromium profile reads), outbound C2, and any ssh.exe reverse-tunnel; sweep fleet for %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\WindowsHelper\" or (ProcessCommandLine has "module.pyw" and ProcessCommandLine has "WindowsHelper")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\python.exe","\\pythonw.exe")
| where NewProcessName has @"\WindowsHelper\" or (CommandLine has "module.pyw" and CommandLine has "WindowsHelper")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BusySnake Stealer module.pyw Executed From WindowsHelper Directory

BusySnake VBScript persistence: wh_selfdelete.vbs / run.vbs in WindowsHelper AIInstallation High
Hunts the BusySnake persistence and cleanup VBScripts — wh_selfdelete.vbs (wipes the pnx.exe loader) and run.vbs (launches module.pyw and registers the 5-minute scheduled task) — executed by wscript/cscript from the %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper directory. Article-specific by the unique script names and staging path. Rationale: wh_selfdelete.vbs is a unique, actor-specific filename; run.vbs is scoped with the WindowsHelper staging path to keep it high-fidelity. Directly maps to the article's named persistence/cleanup scripts. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/armored-likho-targets-government.html
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal legacy VBScript coincidentally named run.vbs (mitigated by the WindowsHelper path requirement)
  • Login-script or SCCM automation invoking wscript with a same-named script from a different path
  • Malware analyst re-detonating the extracted scripts
  • Backup/uninstaller tooling that self-deletes via a VBS (would not match the unique wh_selfdelete.vbs name)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\CCM"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the VBS contents and the scheduled-task definition it created (look for the 5-minute recurrence launching module.pyw). 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task and the WindowsHelper directory, isolate the host, and block re-creation. 3) Hunt: verify whether wh_selfdelete.vbs already wiped the pnx.exe loader (check DeviceFileEvents FileDeleted), and pivot to credential/cookie theft and outbound C2 on the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "wh_selfdelete.vbs" or (ProcessCommandLine has "run.vbs" and ProcessCommandLine has "WindowsHelper")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has "wh_selfdelete.vbs" or (CommandLine has "run.vbs" and CommandLine has "WindowsHelper")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BusySnake VBScript Persistence/Cleanup From WindowsHelper

ZDI-CAN-25373 (CVE-2025-9491) LNK spawning PowerShell to fetch BusySnake loader AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Armored Likho LNK infection vector: a malicious shortcut abusing CVE-2025-9491/ZDI-CAN-25373 (whitespace-padded hidden arguments) launched via Explorer, spawning PowerShell that downloads the loader and its python.zip/data.zip/get-pip.py package into WindowsHelper. Article-specific by the parent (explorer→powershell from LNK) plus the named payload artifacts. Rationale: Combines the CVE-2025-9491 LNK vector (Explorer-parented PowerShell) with the article's named loader-package artifacts (python.zip, data.zip, get-pip.py, WindowsHelper), which are specific to this chain rather than generic download cradles. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-9491 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2025/10/31/zdi-can-25373-cve-2025-9491-exploited-again/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/IT shortcut that legitimately invokes PowerShell to fetch a zip package (rare and unlikely to reference these exact names)
  • Software updater launched from a Start-Menu LNK downloading a data.zip
  • Red-team/purple-team emulation of the LNK chain
  • User double-clicking a benign .lnk that runs a packaging script referencing get-pip.py
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr","DownloadFile","DownloadString","curl","wget","Start-BitsTransfer","http")
Response runbook
1) Triage: recover the LNK file and inspect its full Target/arguments for whitespace-padded hidden commands (CVE-2025-9491); identify the download URL(s) and originating email/archive. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the PowerShell tree, block the download domains at proxy/DNS, and quarantine the LNK and delivered archive. 3) Hunt: search mail/gateway for the sibling lure archives (zayavka_*.rar, *_psihologicheskiy_test.zip), and pivot to WindowsHelper staging and scheduled-task persistence fleet-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("python.zip","data.zip","get-pip.py","WindowsHelper")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("python.zip","data.zip","get-pip.py","WindowsHelper")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: LNK-Triggered PowerShell Fetching BusySnake Loader Package

BusySnake reverse SSH tunnel: ssh.exe -R launched by bundled Python payload AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the BusySnake reverse-SSH-tunneling remote-access capability (successor to the group's Go2Tunnel usage): an ssh.exe reverse-tunnel (-R) process spawned by the malware's Python interpreter or from the WindowsHelper working directory. Article-specific by the parent-process pivot on the BusySnake payload rather than a generic ssh usage. Rationale: Uses the article's reverse-SSH-tunnel capability and pivots on the BusySnake Python payload (pythonw.exe / module.pyw / WindowsHelper) as parent, so it fires on attacker-driven tunnels rather than routine admin SSH. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/busysnake-stealer-malware/ • https://www.securityweek.com/armored-likho-apt-targeting-government-electric-power-entities/
ATT&CKT1572 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/DevOps engineer running Python automation (Fabric, Ansible, paramiko wrappers) that shells out to ssh -R for legitimate tunneling
  • CI/CD agent using a Python build script to open a reverse tunnel to a jump host
  • Data scientist using a Python-launched ssh -R for remote port forwarding to a lab box
  • Legitimate portable Python tool that manages SSH tunnels
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","fabric","paramiko")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the ssh.exe command line to identify the remote tunnel endpoint (host/port) and confirm the parent is the BusySnake pythonw.exe/module.pyw. 2) Contain: kill the ssh.exe and parent Python process, isolate the host, and block the tunnel destination IP/port at the firewall. 3) Hunt: enumerate all reverse-tunnel destinations across the fleet, correlate with WindowsHelper staging and credential/cookie theft, and review for lateral movement through the tunnel.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ssh.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(^|\s)-R(\s|$)"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "module.pyw" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\WindowsHelper\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\ssh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(^|\s)-R(\s|$)"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\python.exe","\\pythonw.exe") or CommandLine has "WindowsHelper"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Reverse SSH Tunnel Spawned By BusySnake Python Payload

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — How We Added WebAuthn to a Browser-Based RDP Client
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

`o365_management_activity`

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a self-hosted CI/CD runner process (Runner.Worker/node/python/curl) reaching gist.githubusercontent.com — the exact egress the compromised tj-actions/changed-files action used to pull its memory-dumping Python second stage. This was StepSecurity Harden-Runner's original detection signal for the March 2025 incident. Rationale: Uses the corroborated network IOC (outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com from a runner) that StepSecurity's Harden-Runner used to detect CVE-2025-30066; scoped to runner process ancestry (Runner.Worker/node/python/_actions paths) to separate it from ordinary developer gist fetches. Cross-checked against CISA, Wiz and Sysdig write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build step legitimately curls a config/install script hosted on a GitHub gist
  • Developer tooling or dotfiles bootstrap that pulls from gist.githubusercontent.com on a self-hosted runner
  • Package post-install hooks fetching helper scripts from a gist
  • Security tooling / EDR test harness deliberately reaching gist domains
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation resolving raw gist content
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("renovate","dependabot") or RemoteUrl has "raw.githubusercontent.com/your-org")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and parent chain of the initiating process; confirm it ran inside a GitHub Actions job (Runner.Worker/_work/_actions path) and identify the workflow/repo. Grab the exact gist URL and the resolved IP. 2) Contain: if the job used tj-actions/changed-files (or any action pinned to a mutable tag), pause the runner, and immediately rotate every secret exposed to workflows that ran between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC (access keys, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, RSA keys). 3) Hunt: search the same runner fleet for the malicious commit 0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67 and for double-base64 blobs written to workflow logs; review runner egress for other first-seen domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or RemoteUrl has "gist.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","python.exe","python3","python","curl.exe","curl","wget","Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker")
     or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker","node.exe","node")
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("actions-runner","_work","_actions")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or HttpHostName in~ ("gist.githubusercontent.com","gist.github.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066) AIDelivery High
Alerts on the exact malicious tj-actions/changed-files commit SHA (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67) appearing in any process command line or file path on a self-hosted runner — i.e. the compromised action being fetched, checked out, or pinned. A pure, second-source-confirmed IOC hunt for the retagged supply-chain payload. Rationale: Uses the article's SHA1 (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67), independently confirmed by CISA and the GitHub Advisory as the single malicious commit every tj-actions/changed-files tag (v1.0.0–v44.5.1) was pointed to — a unique, zero-ambiguity IOC that only appears when the compromised action is fetched, checked out, or SHA-pinned. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/github-actions-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/threat-intel tooling scanning for the hash as an IOC (grep, EDR IOC sweep) surfaces the string in its own command line
  • A remediation script that greps repos/workflows for the malicious SHA
  • Vulnerability-management agent enumerating the commit as data
  • A security researcher reproducing/analyzing the incident in a lab runner
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("grep.exe","findstr.exe","rg.exe","select-string") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("IOC","threat-intel","scan-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA appears in a real action fetch/checkout (Runner.Worker/git/_actions context) versus an analyst's own IOC-scan process; identify the repo and the workflow run time. 2) Contain: treat the runner and any workflow that executed the action as compromised — rotate all secrets exposed to workflows run between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC, and repin tj-actions/changed-files to the patched v46.0.1 by full SHA. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound gist.githubusercontent.com egress from the same runner, inspect workflow logs for double-base64 secret blobs, and check for the sibling reviewdog/action-setup CVE-2025-30154 across the fleet.
let ioc = "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67";
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has ioc or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ioc
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ProcessEvent", Account=AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
 (DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where FolderPath has ioc or FileName has ioc or FolderPath has "tj-actions/changed-files"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileEvent", Account=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence=FolderPath, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] GitHub Actions runner spawns network tool / interpreter under compromised trivy-action or KICS · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TeamPCP Trivy/KICS supply-chain credential exfil to scan.aquasecurtiy.org & 45.148.10.212 · [LLM] DNS resolution of TeamPCP typosquat exfil domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Credential harvest via /proc/<pid>/mem read of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker
TeamPCP Trivy/KICS supply-chain credential exfil to scan.aquasecurtiy.org & 45.148.10.212 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from CI/CD runners (or any onboarded host) to the exact exfiltration infrastructure used by TeamPCP's compromised aquasecurity/trivy-action and Checkmarx KICS actions. Any egress to these hard IOCs means the credential stealer's POST reached the wire. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim exfil host scan.aquasecurtiy.org (typosquat resolving to 45.148.10.212) plus the pre-extracted secondary IOC IPs/domains; connection to any is near-zero-FP and confirms secrets left the runner.

  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving/probing the IOC domains
  • A blocked/failed connection logged by a proxy that never actually exfiltrated
  • Internal typosquat-monitoring service crawling lookalike domains
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/runner and the InitiatingProcess making the connection; confirm whether it is a CI runner that recently executed aquasecurity/trivy-action or Checkmarx KICS. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, rotate ALL secrets/tokens exposed to that job (GITHUB_TOKEN, cloud OIDC creds, registry creds) and revoke active sessions. 3) Hunt: pull every repo/workflow that referenced the compromised action across the org, pivot on the /proc/pid/mem credential-harvest UC, and block the IOC IPs/domains at egress.

Credential harvest via /proc/<pid>/mem read of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the core TeamPCP payload behaviour: a spawned interpreter (python/node/sh) reading /proc/<pid>/mem of the Runner.Worker process to scrape marked secrets from runner memory. This is the article's exact credential-access primitive, independent of the exfil endpoint. Rationale: Uses the article's exact TTP — a payload process reading /proc/pid/mem of the Runner.Worker process — as the pivot; the Runner.Worker parent + interpreter + /proc/*/mem triad is specific to CI runner memory-scraping and rarely legitimate.
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate profiling/debugging tools (gdb, py-spy) attached to a runner job by a maintainer
  • Crash-dump or coredump collection tooling reading /proc during a CI failure
  • Custom self-hosted-runner health scripts inspecting worker memory usage
  • Security agents themselves reading /proc for telemetry
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("py-spy","gdb","coredumpctl","/usr/bin/perf"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and the target PID; confirm the parent is the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker and the child interpreter is not part of the declared workflow. 2) Contain: kill the job, isolate the runner, and immediately rotate every secret injected into that workflow run plus any downstream cloud OIDC tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate to the C2 egress UC (scan.aquasecurtiy.org/45.148.10.212) within the same job window, and enumerate all repos referencing aquasecurity/trivy-action or Checkmarx KICS by tag.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "Runner.Worker" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Runner.Worker" or ProcessCommandLine has "Runner.Worker"
| where FileName in~ ("python","python3","node","sh","bash","perl","ruby")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ProcessCommandLine has "mem"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "Runner.Worker" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "Runner.Worker"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","node","sh","bash","perl","ruby")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "mem"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GitHub Actions Runner.Worker Memory Scrape via /proc/pid/mem
id: c1d4e7a2-5b62-4f18-8a90-77e3b1c2f6d0
description: Detects an interpreter spawned by the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process reading /proc/<pid>/mem to extract secrets from runner memory, matching TeamPCP's trivy-action credential stealer.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/10-layers-deep-how-stepsecurity-stops-teampcps-trivy-supply-chain-attack-on-github-actions
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1003.007
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|contains: 'Runner.Worker'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/node'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/proc/'
      - 'mem'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(python OR python3 OR node OR bash OR sh OR perl OR ruby) (@process.command_line:*"/proc/"* AND @process.command_line:*mem*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/Runner\.Worker/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(python3?|node|bash|sh|perl|ruby)$/i
| regex("/proc/", field=CommandLine)
| regex("mem", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process has "Runner.Worker" OR Processes.process has "Runner.Worker") AND Processes.process="*/proc/*" AND Processes.process="*mem*" by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process has "Runner.Worker" OR Processes.process has "Runner.Worker") AND Processes.process="*/proc/*" AND Processes.process="*mem*" by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
DNS resolution of TeamPCP typosquat exfil domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS lookups for the misspelled typosquat scan.aquasecurtiy.org (impersonating aquasecurity) and the other TeamPCP staging/exfil domains. Catches the campaign at name-resolution even when egress is blocked or the C2 IP rotates. Rationale: The domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org is an intentional typosquat of aquasecurity called out verbatim in the article; resolving it (or the other named TeamPCP domains) is a high-fidelity, rotation-resistant signal that survives IP changes.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Typosquat-monitoring / brand-protection service resolving lookalike domains
  • Malware sandbox or IOC-validation pipeline resolving the domains
  • Passive-DNS collector or threat-intel feed enrichment
  • DNS sinkhole logging the query after redirect
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying host and the initiating process; determine if it is a CI runner mid-workflow vs a research/monitoring system. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domains org-wide, isolate the runner, and rotate secrets scoped to any workflow that ran on that host. 3) Hunt: pivot to the resolved IP against the C2-connection UC, and check whether the /proc/pid/mem harvest fired on the same host within the job window.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud","tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud","tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub Actions runner spawns network tool / interpreter under compromised trivy-action or KICS AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the execution stage of the supply-chain payload: the Runner.Worker (or a trivy/kics action step) spawning curl/wget/python/node that then reaches the internet — the shape a weaponized aquasecurity/trivy-action or Checkmarx KICS tag exhibits when it stages/exfils. Rationale: Grounds on the article's named compromised actions (aquasecurity/trivy-action, Checkmarx KICS) and the Runner.Worker process; a scanner action shelling out to curl/wget/python for outbound POSTs is off-pattern for legitimate SCA/SBOM tooling.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate trivy DB update fetching vulnerability feeds via curl/wget over HTTPS
  • A workflow step that legitimately uses python/node to post results to an internal dashboard
  • Self-hosted runner bootstrap scripts pulling dependencies
  • Container image scan steps that curl a registry manifest
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("aquasec.com","ghcr.io","github.com","trivy-db","vulnerability-db") and not ProcessCommandLine has "scan.aquasecurtiy")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the ChildProcessCommandLine destination — is it an official aquasecurity/checkmarx endpoint or an unknown/typosquat host? Cross-check the action tag/ref used against the known-compromised list. 2) Contain: cancel the run, isolate the runner, rotate secrets exposed to the job, and pin/replace the action to a verified SHA. 3) Hunt: correlate to the C2, DNS, and /proc/pid/mem UCs on the same host+job, and org-wide enumerate every workflow referencing the compromised action by mutable tag.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "Runner.Worker" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("trivy","trivy-action","kics")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","python","python3","node","nc","ncat")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","-d ","--data","POST","/proc/","scan.aquasecurtiy")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "Runner.Worker" or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("trivy","trivy-action","kics")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","python","python3","node","nc","ncat")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","--data","POST","/proc/","scan.aquasecurtiy")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GitHub Actions Runner Spawns Network Tool Under Trivy/KICS Action
id: e5f6a7b8-1c2d-4e3f-9a0b-6c7d8e9f0a12
description: Detects the Runner.Worker or a trivy/kics action step spawning curl/wget/python/nc making outbound requests, matching the execution stage of TeamPCP's compromised GitHub Actions.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/10-layers-deep-how-stepsecurity-stops-teampcps-trivy-supply-chain-attack-on-github-actions
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|contains:
      - 'Runner.Worker'
      - 'trivy'
      - 'kics'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/node'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(curl OR wget OR python OR python3 OR node OR nc OR ncat) (@process.command_line:*trivy* OR @process.command_line:*kics* OR @process.command_line:*Runner.Worker*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/(Runner\.Worker|trivy|kics)/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(curl|wget|python3?|node|nc|ncat)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process has "Runner.Worker" OR Processes.parent_process="*trivy*" OR Processes.parent_process="*kics*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("curl","wget","python","python3","node","nc","ncat") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process has "Runner.Worker" OR Processes.parent_process="*trivy*" OR Processes.parent_process="*kics*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("curl","wget","python","python3","node","nc","ncat") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.148.10.212", "83.142.209.203", "94.154.172.43") or RemoteUrl has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org", "checkmarx.zone", "models.litellm.cloud", "audit.checkmarx.cx", "tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["45.148.10.212", "83.142.209.203", "94.154.172.43"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["scan.aquasecurtiy.org", "checkmarx.zone", "models.litellm.cloud", "audit.checkmarx.cx", "tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33634")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33634")

9router API key / secret exfiltration via /api/settings/database without prior login AIActions on Objectives Medium
After forging a session cookie, the attacker reads stored provider API keys and auth tokens from 9router's /api/settings/database endpoint. This correlates access to the settings/secret endpoints against the source ever having performed a successful POST /api/auth/login — a forged-token holder never logs in, so absence of a login is the tell. Rationale: Targets the article's named exfiltration path /api/settings/database ("steal valuable API Key, Auth Token") and the operational fact that a forged cookie bypasses the login flow entirely — so a leftanti against successful POST /api/auth/login isolates forged sessions. Sigma/Datadog/Defender/Falcon empty: this is a multi-event correlation on web-tier logs, not a single-event or endpoint signal. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-49352/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jphh-m39h-6gwx
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin session where the login POST landed outside the lookback window or was logged by a different proxy node (login not observed for that src)
  • Automation / IaC that reads 9router settings using a long-lived valid cookie and never re-authenticates in-window
  • Shared NAT egress where one user logged in and another admin IP-shares the same source address
  • Health-check or config-backup jobs polling /api/settings
Suppression filter
// Exclude known automation egress IPs that legitimately read settings with a persistent session:
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.20.0.15", "10.20.0.16")   // replace with your config-management egress IPs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request sequence for the SrcIpAddr; confirm the auth_token cookie matches the forged shape from UC1 and that no successful /api/auth/login exists for it across all proxy nodes. Check HTTP status on /api/settings/database (200 = secrets returned). 2) CONTAIN: Rotate ALL provider API keys and auth tokens held by 9router immediately (treat as disclosed), set JWT_SECRET + restart, block the source IP. 3) HUNT: Check for password-change and shutdown API calls from the same source, and for outbound use of the stolen keys against upstream provider APIs (billing/usage spikes).

| where SrcIpAddr !in (LoggedIn)     // forged-token holder never authenticated
